strengths: The submission is best assessed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, with an additional algorithmic contribution. MMEarth-Bench fills a meaningful gap by providing five globally distributed environmental tasks, 12 consistently aligned modalities, low-data subsets, and both random and continent-held-out test splits.

The dataset construction and documentation are unusually extensive. The manuscript reports sources, licenses, split sizes, units, missing-data rates, target distributions, preprocessing, spatial-overlap removal, and detailed tile-generation procedures. The geographic visualization tool and planned release of data and code further support usability.

The empirical study is broad: seven recent pretrained models spanning RGB, multispectral, and multimodal inputs are evaluated with three training-set sizes, three seeds, full finetuning and linear probing, and random versus geographic testing. The pronounced degradation on Africa for four of five tasks is an important result for geospatial foundation-model research.

TTT-MMR is a sensible and broadly applicable way to exploit test-time modalities that an encoder cannot directly consume. Per-modality gradient normalization and geographic batching are intuitive design choices, and the method is demonstrated across diverse architectures and both regression and multilabel classification.

The paper is generally clear and candid about several findings that complicate its narrative, including weak geographic generalization, cases where multimodal finetuning harms out-of-distribution performance, negative R-squared values, and the substantial inference-time overhead of adaptation.
weaknesses: The algorithmic evaluation lacks strong test-time-adaptation baselines. TTT-MMR is compared principally with finetuning and its own joint-training precursor; dismissing TENT as unsuitable for regression does not replace comparisons with other architecture-agnostic reconstruction, consistency, parameter-efficient, or source-free adaptation methods. Consequently, the evidence supports the usefulness of multimodal reconstruction but not a strong claim of superiority over modern adaptation alternatives.

Important ablations are missing despite being central to the method's stated mechanism: individual or grouped reconstruction modalities, removal of geolocation/biome/ecoregion targets, unnormalized versus normalized gradients, number of update iterations, batch size, decoder capacity, and geographic versus random batching under controlled batch composition. The assertion that combining all 12 losses prevents overfitting and that gradient normalization improves stability is therefore insufficiently substantiated.

Several auxiliary modalities encode location very directly, especially geolocation, biome, and ecoregion. This is particularly consequential for an Africa-held-out split and for species labels derived from geographic range polygons. Without modality ablations or simple coordinate/climate-only baselines, it is unclear how much of the reported gain reflects improved visual representations rather than learning geographic priors or reconstructing metadata.

The geographic benchmark conflates multiple shifts: continent, target-label distribution, environmental conditions, and sampling density. For example, the supplementary statistics show large target-distribution changes between non-Africa and Africa. A single Africa-versus-rest split provides limited evidence about general geographic robustness; multiple held-out regions or spatial cross-validation would make the conclusions substantially stronger. The random split is also not spatially blocked, so spatial autocorrelation may inflate its results.

The species task evaluates agreement with IUCN range polygons rather than independently observed occurrence. Its examples are deliberately sampled from selected species ranges, and one hundred species are chosen as the 'first' entries after filtering. These choices can introduce selection and spatial-prior shortcuts and limit the ecological interpretation of the very high in-distribution scores.

The statistical analysis pools results across models, tasks, and seeds in Wilcoxon tests even though these observations are not independent and the tasks use different metrics. Reporting paired effects and uncertainty separately per task/model, or using an appropriate hierarchical analysis, would better support the generality claims. Raw tables also contain ties and degradations, making statements that the method improves every model, task, and split too strong unless explicitly qualified as aggregate results.

Reproducibility is mostly strong, but some details remain unclear, including masked loss/evaluation for sparse pixel-level biomass targets, treatment of missing modalities during joint training, task-specific selected iteration counts, and complete adaptation hyperparameter sensitivity. The figure describing the method also contains what appears to be an unfinished author note, which should be corrected.

strengths: The benchmark is a substantial contribution: five globally distributed environmental tasks, 12 aligned modalities, low-data subsets, and both random and Africa-held-out test splits.

The evaluation covers seven recent pretrained models spanning RGB, multispectral, and multimodal architectures, plus a random-initialization baseline and three seeds. Raw results and implementation details are extensively reported in the supplement.

TTT-MMR is conceptually simple and broadly applicable: auxiliary modalities can supervise adaptation without being accepted as encoder inputs, and resetting after each batch limits persistent model drift.

The experiments reveal useful findings for Earth-observation research, including severe geographic-generalization gaps and cases where multimodal finetuning improves in-distribution performance while worsening geographic transfer.

Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best viewed as a hybrid Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms contribution. The dataset component is considerably stronger than the algorithmic evidence.
weaknesses: The proposed method is compared only with joint training. There are no competitive test-time adaptation baselines, reconstruction-based TTT baselines, or even controlled single-modality variants. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether multimodal reconstruction, rather than generic additional test-time optimization, causes the gains.

Essential ablations are missing: modality subsets, exclusion of geolocation/biome/ecoregion, gradient normalization, frozen versus updated decoder, batch size, learning rate, number of iterations, and alternative geographic grouping. The claims that 12 losses prevent overfitting and gradient normalization improves stability are asserted without supporting experiments.

Many gains are small for the strongest models. Table S.10 reports relative improvements of only about 0.4–1.0% for Copernicus-FM and TerraMind in several settings, while Tables S.15–S.30 contain cases of unchanged or degraded individual results. Average ranks obscure these effect sizes, making the broad claim of improvement across all models, tasks, and splits too strong.

The significance analysis pools models and seeds in one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Different architectures are not independent experimental replicates, and seeds within an architecture also do not justify treating all observations as exchangeable. The paper should report paired effects and uncertainty per model/task and correct over the full family of comparisons.

The benchmark splits do not adequately control spatial dependence. Non-African samples are randomly assigned to training and random-test sets, despite strong spatial autocorrelation in environmental variables. For the species task, points are explicitly sampled from the same IUCN range polygons and overlapping ranges determine labels, so nearby train/test samples can make the random split particularly easy. Spatially blocked validation and multiple held-out regions are needed.

The sole geographic evaluation equates Africa with out-of-distribution generalization. It simultaneously changes geography, label distributions, sample sizes, and sampling coverage; for example, soil geographic sets contain only 232–349 samples and their target statistics differ markedly from training. This makes it difficult to attribute failures or improvements specifically to geographic adaptation and limits global conclusions.

Several auxiliary targets—geolocation, biome, ecoregion, climate, land-cover products, and canopy height—are privileged covariates strongly related to the downstream labels. Their individual contributions and availability assumptions are not analyzed. Acquiring all 12 modalities through Earth Engine also weakens the claimed model-agnostic practicality for ordinary deployment.
The method is described as efficient, but Table S.8 shows roughly 78–184 times the cost of a standard forward pass. No memory analysis or accuracy–compute comparison is provided.

Dataset validity needs deeper treatment. Soil measurements aggregated across time are paired with 2020 imagery, while the species labels come from coarse historical range polygons rather than observed occurrences. These limitations, potential label noise, licensing restrictions, and appropriate-use boundaries are insufficiently discussed.

strengths: The submission is best assessed as a hybrid Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms/General contribution. Its strongest component is MMEarth-Bench: five environmentally meaningful tasks, 12 consistently aligned modalities, global coverage, low-data subsets, and both random and held-out-region evaluations. This fills a credible gap in Earth-observation benchmarking.

The benchmark study is unusually broad, covering seven recent pretrained models with RGB, multispectral, and multimodal inputs, plus a randomly initialized baseline. Experiments span five tasks, three training-set sizes, two test splits, and three seeds, with raw results and implementation details supplied in the supplement.

The geographic evaluation produces useful findings beyond model ranking: pretrained models still fail badly on several Africa splits, multimodal pretraining is generally beneficial, and learned multimodal fusion can sometimes exacerbate geographic overfitting. These observations are relevant to both computer vision and practical environmental monitoring.

TTT-MMR is simple, model-agnostic in spirit, applicable to both regression and classification, and exploits modalities that need not be accepted as encoder inputs. Improvements over joint training are consistent across the reported models, tasks, and splits, while geographic batching is a sensible way to balance local specialization and gradient regularization.

The manuscript is clear and well organized. The supplement gives substantial dataset-construction detail, split sizes, missing-data statistics, licenses, normalization procedures, complete numerical results, and inference-time measurements, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method evaluation lacks sufficiently strong adaptation baselines. TTT-MMR and its geographic variant are compared primarily with joint training, but not with a broader set of architecture-compatible test-time adaptation, self-training, or reconstruction-based alternatives. Consequently, the experiments establish that test-time reconstruction updates help, but do not clearly establish that the proposed formulation is preferable to existing adaptation strategies.

Several central method choices are not ablated: using all 12 reconstruction targets versus subsets, per-modality gradient normalization, decoder design, batch size, number of iterations, encoder resetting, and random versus geographic batches at matched spatial diversity. In particular, the claims that combining modalities prevents overfitting and that gradient normalization improves stability are asserted without quantitative evidence.

The geographic-generalization evidence uses only one held-out macro-region, Africa. Moreover, the target distributions differ substantially between random and geographic splits—for example, the supplementary statistics show large biomass and soil-organic-carbon mean shifts. This is a realistic challenge but makes it difficult to separate geographic covariate shift, label shift, and region-specific difficulty, limiting the breadth of the generalization claims.

Geolocation, biome, and ecoregion are included among the reconstruction targets. These variables can be strongly predictive of the environmental labels and directly encode the geographic partition. Modality-wise ablations are needed to determine whether the adaptation gains reflect genuinely improved visual representations or primarily stronger localization. This is especially important for the species task, whose labels are derived from spatially smooth IUCN range polygons rather than direct occurrence observations.

The statistical presentation could be more rigorous. Rank summaries obscure the fact that gains for some strong models are very small, only three seeds are used, and the effective independent units and paired structure underlying the Wilcoxon tests are not clearly specified. Per-task confidence intervals and corrected tests at the model-task level would make the evidence easier to assess.

The claim of efficient adaptation should be qualified: the reported TTT inference times are roughly two orders of magnitude above a standard forward pass, even if they remain below one second per sample on an H200. Practical evaluation for streaming, single-sample, or resource-constrained deployment is absent, and several dataset licenses or terms of use may also restrict downstream redistribution.

strengths: The paper makes a substantial hybrid Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms contribution: MMEarth-Bench adds five globally distributed environmental tasks with 12 aligned modalities, low-data subsets, and both random and continent-held-out test splits. This fills a meaningful gap in existing Earth-observation benchmarks.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. Eight recent pretrained models plus randomly initialized baselines are evaluated across five tasks, three training-set sizes, and two test regimes. The finding that multimodal pretraining helps most with limited labels, yet can be matched by training from scratch with sufficient data, is useful and appropriately nuanced.

TTT-MMR is simple, architecture-agnostic, and applicable to both regression and multi-label classification. Its use of auxiliary modalities as reconstruction targets is well motivated, and improvements are reported across diverse encoder families, tasks, and splits with three seeds and paired significance tests.

The geographic batching variant is intuitive, and the long-tail analysis suggests a potentially valuable benefit beyond average performance. The appendix also reports raw results, relative improvements, iteration counts, leave-one-modality-out analysis, reconstruction quality, runtime, data-generation details, and hyperparameters.

The manuscript is clearly organized and visually polished. Dataset construction, missing-data handling, licenses, evaluation metrics, and the interfaces used for different pretrained models are documented in considerable detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The algorithmic evaluation lacks competitive test-time adaptation baselines. Joint training is the only direct baseline, despite the discussion of masked-reconstruction TTT, TENT, S4T, and other approaches. Even where some methods do not directly support regression or transformer encoders, comparisons on the compatible classification/model settings or adapted reconstruction baselines are needed to establish that the gains come from the proposed multimodal design rather than generic test-time optimization.

Key method components are insufficiently ablated. The paper does not isolate per-modality gradient normalization, updating the full encoder versus restricted parameters, multimodal versus a single reconstruction target, frozen versus updated reconstruction heads, or alternative spatial batching strategies. The leave-one-modality-out experiment on only DINOv3 Sat and one seed does not validate the claim that averaging 12 normalized gradients is responsible for stability.

The practical gains for the strongest models are often extremely small. Table A.17 includes improvements near zero, while Table A.15 shows negative average relative improvement for Galileo or ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split. This makes the broad language that TTT improves all models, tasks, and splits too strong and suggests that headline boxplots are partly driven by weaker RGB models.

The geographic split holds out all of Africa, simultaneously changing geography, label distributions, sampling density, biome/ecoregion composition, and potentially modality quality. It is a valuable stress test but does not isolate geographic covariate shift, and evidence from one held-out continent is insufficient for broad conclusions about global geographic generalization. Multiple held-out regions or leave-one-region-out evaluation would strengthen the benchmark.

The random train/validation/test split only prevents tile overlap; geographically adjacent samples may still occur across splits. Given strong spatial autocorrelation in environmental variables and coarse species-range polygons, this can inflate in-distribution and low-shot results. A spatially blocked non-African split would be a more informative complement.

The species task uses membership in IUCN range polygons rather than observed occurrence, so calling its labels “species occurrence” is potentially misleading. Range polygons can be coarse and encode expert-derived geographic priors, while geolocation, biome, and ecoregion are supplied as modalities. The paper should characterize polygon uncertainty and clarify that the task predicts mapped range membership.

Several auxiliary products may be very close proxies for the targets—for example, global canopy height for GEDI biomass—and some are themselves derived model products. This is a legitimate multimodal setting, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss target-proxy dependence, possible upstream data overlap, or whether improvements represent transferable visual adaptation versus exploitation of derived geospatial products.

TTT-MMR is roughly two orders of magnitude slower than a forward pass and geographic batching assumes access to and spatial organization of a test collection. These deployment constraints, along with non-commercial licensing for the soil data and IUCN terms for species data, limit the benchmark’s practical reuse and deserve a more explicit limitations discussion.

strengths: The work is best viewed as a hybrid Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms contribution. MMEarth-Bench is substantial: five newly assembled environmental tasks, 12 aligned modalities, global coverage, low-data subsets, and both random and Africa-held-out evaluations.

Dataset construction, preprocessing, missing-data statistics, licenses, split sizes, hyperparameters, per-seed results, and raw metrics are documented unusually thoroughly, supporting reproducibility and diagnostic use.

The benchmark covers eight recent pretrained models plus randomly initialized baselines, revealing useful findings about low-shot transfer, multimodal inputs, and the severe geographic-generalization gap.

Using otherwise incompatible test-time modalities as reconstruction targets is an intuitive and potentially useful adaptation mechanism. The method applies to regression as well as classification and is demonstrated across diverse encoder architectures.
The paper is generally well organized, clearly written, and includes useful modality ablations, iteration analyses, reconstruction diagnostics, and inference-time measurements.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated. The paper says TTT improves all models, tasks, and splits, but the raw tables contain multiple degradations, and Appendix Table A.15 reports negative average relative improvements for Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split. For the best model per task, several gains are effectively zero or smaller than their reported uncertainty, including 0.00000 ± 0.00057 for soil organic carbon and 0.00010 ± 0.00001 mAP for species.

The method comparison is inadequate. TTT-MMR is evaluated primarily against joint training, without competitive generic TTT approaches such as masked-reconstruction TTT, suitable entropy or pseudo-label baselines for classification, or modular late-fusion/adapter methods that can exploit the same auxiliary modalities. Consequently, it is unclear whether gains arise from the proposed gradient-normalized TTT mechanism or simply from granting additional test-time information.

The benchmark has serious spatial-confounding risks. Its random split only prohibits overlapping 1.28 km tiles and applies no geographic buffer or spatially blocked partition; explicit geolocation, biome, and ecoregion are also inputs. Nearby train and test examples can therefore share strong spatial signals. This is especially problematic for the species task, whose labels are generated from IUCN range polygons rather than independent observations and reaches approximately 0.99 random-split mAP, suggesting interpolation or memorization of geographic ranges rather than visual species inference.

The single geographic split equates geographic generalization with transfer to Africa. It cannot establish general geographic robustness, and the African soil test sets are small (232–349 samples) with substantially different target distributions. Region effects, label shift, sample-size effects, and genuine covariate adaptation are therefore conflated. Multiple held-out continents or spatial cross-validation would make the benchmark conclusions much stronger.

The statistical evidence is not fully convincing. The Wilcoxon tests appear to pool heterogeneous model/seed results, whose independence is questionable, while only three seeds are used. The long-tail result in Figure 8 uses just one seed. Per-task and per-model uncertainty or hierarchical testing is needed, particularly because many improvements are tiny.

Claims of model- and task-agnosticism are broader than the evidence: all five tasks come from one Earth-observation pipeline with the same modalities, four are environmental regression problems, and all test-time experiments assume access to the full auxiliary modality set.

The method is described as efficient, yet five TTT iterations increase measured inference from 0.002–0.009 to 0.367–0.910 seconds per sample, roughly 80–180 times for the reported models. It also depends on batch composition, geographic metadata, and resetting the encoder for each batch. These practical constraints and the possibility of harmful adaptation deserve clearer treatment.

The dataset documentation is strong, but reproducibility still depends on a large university-hosted dataset, Google Earth Engine processing, substantial H200 training, and data with heterogeneous licenses, including noncommercial soil data and unspecified species 'Terms of Use'. Long-term hosting, redistribution rights, and exact public release commitments should be clarified.

strengths: The paper makes a substantial contribution to Earth-observation vision through MMEarth-Bench: five newly constructed environmental tasks, 12 consistently aligned modalities, globally distributed samples, low-label subsets, and both random and geographic test splits. I assess it primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an additional algorithmic component, which strengthens the case for acceptance.

The benchmark addresses an important and insufficiently studied question: whether globally pretrained geospatial models actually generalize to regions without downstream labels. The pronounced Africa generalization gaps on four of five tasks are informative negative results for the community.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering eight recent pretrained models with RGB, multispectral, and multimodal inputs, two randomly initialized controls, five tasks, three training-set sizes, two test splits, and three seeds. The strong randomly initialized multimodal baseline yields a useful conclusion about the relative roles of pretraining and modality access.

TTT-MMR is simple, architecture-agnostic, and applicable to both classification and regression. Per-modality gradient normalization and geographic batching are sensible design choices, and improvements are demonstrated across diverse encoder families. The geographic-batching results on rare targets are particularly interesting.

The manuscript is technically clear and well organized. It provides formalization, dataset-generation details, normalization and missing-data statistics, hyperparameters, full numerical results, modality ablations, iteration counts, inference costs, reconstruction analyses, and linear-probing results. Three-seed reporting and corrected Wilcoxon tests further strengthen the empirical presentation.

The dataset explorer and stated code/data release could make the work a valuable community resource. The paper also appropriately reports difficult and negative findings rather than presenting benchmark saturation.
weaknesses: The method evaluation lacks comparisons to alternative test-time adaptation or self-supervised adaptation methods. Joint training is the only central baseline, so the experiments establish that test-time reconstruction updates help over no test-time update, but do not clearly establish TTT-MMR's advantage over other applicable reconstruction-, consistency-, or parameter-efficient adaptation strategies.

The practical gains for already strong models are often very small. For the best model selected per task, Table A.17 reports improvements as low as 0.0000-0.0123, with several geographic-split standard errors comparable to the gains. Table A.15 also shows negative average relative improvements for Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split. Consequently, claims that all models benefit and that performance improves across all model-task-split combinations are stronger than the detailed results support.

The geographic evaluation consists of one particular shift—training outside Africa and testing in Africa. This is important, but it conflates geographic transfer with continent-specific label and sampling differences and does not show that conclusions hold for other held-out regions. Moreover, the random split prevents tile overlap but apparently does not impose a spatial buffer, so nearby train and test tiles may make the in-distribution baseline optimistic.

Some tasks admit strong shortcuts through the supplied auxiliary products. Canopy height is closely related to biomass, while geolocation, biome, and ecoregion can be highly predictive of species range labels. The species task is generated from IUCN historic range polygons rather than point observations of actual occurrence. These choices are legitimate for multimodal benchmarking, but the paper should more clearly delimit ecological interpretations and quantify performance with shortcut-prone modalities removed jointly, rather than only one-at-a-time ablations for one model and seed.

TTT-MMR assumes that all 12 modalities can be acquired at inference time and requires roughly 40-180 times the cost of a standard forward pass in the reported examples. Several modalities are themselves processed global products, so applicability under latency, data-access, or sensor-availability constraints is narrower than the model-agnostic framing suggests.

Reusability may be constrained by the CC BY-NC licenses for the soil tasks and unspecified Terms of Use for the species task. The project-page link is also blank in the submitted PDF, preventing verification of the promised dataset, code, and visualization tool during review.
